title: Unraveling Bilateral Ptosis: A 16-Year-Old's Diagnostic Journey
summary: This poster details the clinical evaluation of a 16-year-old male presenting with severe bilateral ptosis. It meticulously covers the examination findings, the differential diagnostic process including suspicion of myasthenia gravis, and the specific tests performed, culminating in a diagnosis of bilateral congenital ptosis. Essential ophthalmic measurements and broader differential diagnoses for ptosis are also highlighted.

sections.title: Patient Presentation & Initial Inspection
content: **2-Examine 16 years old male patient with Bilateral severe ptosis**.
- No lid crease (classic for congenital ptosis)

sections.title: The Diagnostic Conundrum: Suspecting Myasthenia Gravis
sections.content: The discussion continued: 'then ask for causes no anisocoria, EOM is full'. The examiner then asked 'what else in examination'. The student was confused, so the examiner prompted: 'what other cause you suspect'. The student responded: 'I said may be myasthenia gravis'.

sections.title: How to Perform Myasthenia Gravis Tests
content: - Apply an ice pack (or ice-filled glove) to the closed eyelids for 2-5 minutes.

- Observe for improvement in ptosis, which is considered positive if lid elevation increases by ≥2 mm. Cold reduces acetylcholinesterase activity, allowing more acetylcholine to act at the neuromuscular junction.
- Ask the patient to maintain sustained upgaze (looking up without moving their head) for 30-60 seconds.
- Observe for increasing ptosis (fatigue) or saccadic pursuit movements.
- Ask the patient to rapidly look down from primary gaze, then back to primary gaze.

- Observe for a brief, transient twitch or overshoot of the upper eyelid, followed by a quick return to its ptotic position. This is due to activation of the hyperactive frontalis in an attempt to compensate for weakness, followed by rapid fatigue of the levator.

sections.title: The Final Diagnosis
content: After the examination and tests, the examiner asked 'what your diagnosis'. The student responded: 'I told bilateral congenital ptosis'.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Levator Function & Ptosis Classification

content.explanation: MRD1 (Margin Reflex Distance 1) measures the distance from the corneal light reflex to the upper lid margin in primary gaze (normal 4-5 mm). MRD2 (Margin Reflex Distance 2) measures the distance from the corneal light reflex to the lower lid margin (normal ~5 mm). Levator Excursion (Levator Function) is the range of upper lid movement from extreme downgaze to extreme upgaze, while the frontalis muscle is immobilized (forehead held). A Levator Excursion of 17 mm is considered **excellent** and strongly suggests intact levator muscle function, directing diagnosis towards aponeurotic or congenital etiologies rather than myogenic or neurogenic causes with poor function. In congenital ptosis, good levator function with absent lid crease often indicates a dystrophic levator muscle, not true paralysis.

rows: Congenital
Simple Congenital Ptosis, Blepharophimosis Syndrome (BPES)

Present at birth, often bilateral. Absent/poor lid crease, frontalis overaction, good levator function (dystrophic muscle), chin-up head posture. BPES includes telecanthus, epicanthus inversus, ectropion of lower lids.
Myogenic
Myasthenia Gravis (MG), Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia (CPEO), Oculopharyngeal Muscular Dystrophy (OPMD), Myotonic Dystrophy

MG: Fluctuating ptosis, fatigability (worsens with sustained effort), Cogan's twitch, ophthalmoplegia. CPEO: Symmetrical, slowly progressive ptosis & EOM restriction (often without diplopia), +/- orbicularis weakness. OPMD: Ptosis, dysphagia. Myotonic Dystrophy: Ptosis, facial weakness, Christmas tree cataract, myotonia.
Neurogenic
Bilateral Oculomotor Nerve Palsy (rare), Bilateral Horner's Syndrome (very rare)

Oculomotor Palsy: Ptosis with significant EOM restriction (up, down, in), mydriasis. Horner's: Mild ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis. Bilateral presentation of these is highly unusual and suggests systemic neurological pathology (e.g., brainstem lesion, severe trauma).
Aponeurotic
Involutional Ptosis (rarely bilateral simultaneously), Post-operative
Most common in elderly, usually unilateral. Good levator function, high lid crease. Rarely bilateral with age or following bilateral cataract surgery/trauma.
Mechanical/Inflammatory
Orbital Tumor (e.g., lymphoma), Edema (e.g., thyroid eye disease), Orbital Fat Prolapse
Associated mass, pain, proptosis, restricted EOMs. Ptosis can be due to weight, inflammation, or restriction of levator.
Systemic Toxins/Drugs
Botulism, Diphtheria, Opioids, Sedatives, Anticholinergics
Rapid onset, often associated with systemic neurological signs (e.g., dilated pupils, dysphagia, generalized weakness).
Pseudoptosis
Dermatochalasis (redundant skin), Hypotropia (lower eye gives illusion of ptosis in the other eye), Contralateral lid retraction
Not true ptosis of the levator. Careful examination distinguishes these from true eyelid drooping.

sections.title: Ptosis Red Flags: Urgent Considerations
content: **Acute Onset Ptosis:** Especially if painful or associated with diplopia, headache, pupillary changes (anisocoria, mydriasis). Could indicate aneurysmal compression of CN III (pupil-involving CN III palsy is a neuro-ophthalmic emergency).
**Progressive Ptosis with Diplopia/Weakness:** Suggests neuromuscular junction disorders (Myasthenia Gravis) or progressive external ophthalmoplegia.
**Ptosis with New-Onset Anisocoria:** Horner's syndrome (miosis, mild ptosis, anhidrosis) or CN III palsy (mydriasis, ptosis, EOM restriction).
**Associated with Systemic Symptoms:** Generalized weakness, difficulty swallowing or breathing, speech changes – consider botulism, myasthenia crisis, or other systemic neurological disorders.
**Proptosis or Orbital Signs:** Suggestive of an orbital mass, inflammation, or infection.
